topic: Blue sunsets on Mars: dust scattering, butterscotch daytime sky, Curiosity 2015 image
hook: Sunsets on Mars are blue, not red.

slides.title: A reversed sky
slides.body: By day, the Martian sky looks butterscotch. At sunset, a cold blue glow forms around the sun.
slides.image_prompt: A small pale sun setting over a rocky reddish desert, surrounded by a cold blue halo fading into a dusty butterscotch sky

slides.title: Blame the dust
slides.body: Fine Martian dust is just the right size to let blue light pass through slightly more easily near the sun.
slides.image_prompt: Fine red dust drifting in the air above a cracked Martian surface, a faint blue light passing through the haze

slides.title: Earth does the opposite
slides.body: Our air scatters blue across the whole sky. At sunset, light travels so far that mostly reds and oranges remain.
slides.image_prompt: A vivid orange and red sunset over a calm ocean horizon, deep blue sky fading at the top
slides.credit: Rick Curran (CC0 / public domain) via openverse

slides.title: Caught on camera
slides.body: NASA's Curiosity rover photographed a blue sunset in Gale Crater in April 2015.
slides.image_prompt: A six-wheeled rover on a rocky Martian crater floor at dusk, a small blue-tinted sun sinking behind distant crater rim

caption:
On Mars, the colors of the sky are flipped. Daytime looks hazy butterscotch, but as the sun goes down, a blue glow gathers around it.

NASA's Curiosity rover captured this in Gale Crater in April 2015. Fine dust in the thin Martian air lets blue light through near the sun's direction. Follow for one surprising, verified fact every day. Source: NASA/JPL.

Would you rather watch a sunset on Mars or on Earth?
